help.title: Help
help.subtitle: What the numbers mean
help.intro: Everything here is measured on this machine and stays on it. Nothing on this page is fetched from anywhere — it ships with the app, so it reads the same whether or not you can reach the internet.

ping.title: Why this is not the ping your game shows
ping.short: Your game times its own packets. This app cannot read them, so it shows two different, honest numbers instead.
ping.body: Your game shows a number it measures itself: it sends a packet only its own server can answer, in its own language, and times the reply inside the game. Nothing outside the game can reproduce that. Reading it would mean speaking the game's protocol, capturing packets with a driver, or reading the game's memory — and all three are refused here. Two of them are exactly what anti-cheat systems are built to detect, and none of them is safe for you. So this app measures two things it can measure honestly, and never merges them into one number: the round trip to the deepest router that answers on the way to the server, and the pattern of the traffic your game is actually exchanging. Neither is the round trip to the server, and the app never claims otherwise. Their disagreement is what makes them useful: a clean route with ragged arrivals points at the server, and a ragged route with even arrivals usually means a router is deprioritising our probes rather than that anything is wrong with your game.

rtt.title: Ping (RTT)
rtt.short: The round trip of a probe we send to this endpoint: out and back, in milliseconds. The same quantity other tools call ping.
rtt.body: The app sends its own small probe and times the reply. That is the round-trip time — RTT — and it is the same quantity every other network tool calls ping: a real round trip over the route your application is using, and the most direct figure on the page where it exists. It is not the number your game shows in its own corner: the game times its own packets to its own server, which nothing outside the game can reproduce. Where an endpoint answers nothing we can send — the normal state of a game's match server, because nothing listens on a game port but the game — this figure is not shown at all, and the route and the traffic figures stand in for it instead.

jitter.title: Jitter
jitter.short: How much the round trip varies between probes. A steady 80 ms usually plays better than a 40 ms that jumps.
jitter.body: Two connections with the same average round trip can feel completely different. What you notice while playing is not the average but the variation: a connection that answers in 40 ms and then 90 ms and then 45 ms makes a game stutter, while a steady 80 ms feels smooth. Jitter is that variation, measured over the recent window. Lower is better, and a large jitter beside a small average is worth more attention than a large average on its own. Where the traffic itself is being watched you will see a second figure called arrival jitter: that one is measured from your game's own incoming data rather than from our probes, and the two are kept apart on purpose.

loss.title: Loss
loss.short: The share of our probes that never came back. Blank where the endpoint does not answer probes at all.
loss.body: The share of the probes this app sent that produced no reply, over the recent window — packet loss, measured on our own probes. It describes those probes on the route they took, not necessarily your game's own packets, which travel as their own traffic. Where nothing answers our probes at all, this stays blank instead of reading as 100 %: a server that ignores what we send is not a server that is dropping your game's traffic, and reporting one as the other would be the exact mistake this app exists to avoid.

route.title: The route towards it
route.short: The round trip to the last router that answers on the way to the server — not to the server itself.
route.body: When an endpoint answers nothing, the app measures the deepest router on the way to it that does answer, and watches that router continuously. This usually reaches the edge of the datacentre the server sits in, so it covers almost the whole path — but not the last step, and how long that step takes is unknown. That is why it is never shown as the round trip to the server. What it is good for: it tells you whether the part of the path you can do something about is healthy, and where it stops if it is not — inside your own network, inside your provider, or somewhere beyond.

updates.title: Updates from the server
updates.short: How many times a second the server sends your game something. Steady is what matters, not high.
updates.body: Counted from the traffic itself: how often data arrives from this endpoint, with the packets of a single update counted once. Most games settle at a fixed rate. The useful reading is not the number itself but whether it holds: a rate that drops while your own sending continues means the server or the path towards you has stopped keeping up.

arrivalJitter.title: Arrival jitter
arrivalJitter.short: How evenly your game's own incoming data arrives. Jitter measured on the traffic itself, not on a probe — and this is what you feel as stutter.
arrivalJitter.body: Updates that arrive every 50 ms feel smooth; the same number of updates arriving in bursts does not. Arrival jitter is how much the gaps between arrivals vary, and it is the closest thing on this page to what you actually feel while playing. It is called arrival jitter rather than jitter because it is a different measurement from the jitter beside the round trip: that one times replies to probes we sent, this one is taken from data your game is already receiving, without sending anything. It cannot separate a network that delayed a packet from a server that skipped a tick — both look identical from here — which is why it is shown beside the route rather than instead of it. When the route is clean and this is ragged, the server is the better explanation.

worstPause.title: Worst pause
worstPause.short: The longest gap between two updates in the window — the single worst hitch.
worstPause.body: The longest the traffic went quiet between two arrivals during the window. An average hides exactly the moment you noticed, so this reports the worst one instead. A worst pause several times the usual gap is a hitch you would have felt, even if every average on the page looks reasonable.

dropOff.title: Drop-off
dropOff.short: How far the incoming traffic has fallen below what this endpoint was recently doing. Deliberately not called loss — it is a different measurement from the loss figure.
dropOff.body: This compares what is arriving now with what this same endpoint was sending a short while ago, while what you send holds steady. It is not packet loss, and it is careful not to claim to be — which is also why it does not share a name with the loss figure beside the round trip: that one counts probes we sent and can therefore say exactly how many came back, while only the far end knows what it sent here, so a packet that never arrived is invisible from this side. What can be said is that noticeably less is coming back than this connection itself established as normal — which is a real finding, and a different one from a measured loss figure.

freeze.title: Freeze
freeze.short: Your game is still sending and nothing has come back for this long.
freeze.body: A one-way outage, seen without sending a single probe: your application is still sending to this endpoint and nothing has arrived back for the stated time. It appears only while your own traffic continues, because a silence of yours says nothing about theirs. This is the strongest evidence on the page that something is actually wrong right now, and it is the one figure here a player recognises immediately.

traffic.title: Data exchanged
traffic.short: How many bytes crossed this connection recently. A count over a stated window, not a speed.
traffic.body: How much data the operating system counted crossing this connection in the recent window. It is a count rather than a rate, because the window it covers is approximate and dividing would invent a precision the measurement does not have. Its main use is telling apart the connection your game plays over — which carries a great deal — from a launcher or a telemetry host, which barely carry anything.

probeKind.title: How it is being measured
probeKind.short: Which kind of probe produced the numbers. Different kinds measure slightly different things.
probeKind.body: The app tries the cheapest honest probe first and falls back when it is refused. An echo is the plainest round trip. A connection attempt measures a round trip plus the far end deciding to accept it. A handshake probe measures the round trip end to end through a tunnel, where the two cheaper kinds would measure only as far as the tunnel and report a falsely good number. "Filtering confirmed" means a kind was proven blocked — a later kind succeeded where it failed — which is knowledge, unlike silence. "Through a tunnel" means something on your network redirects this address, so the figure covers the whole tunnelled path rather than a round trip to the server.

age.title: Age
age.short: How long this endpoint has been there — which tells one that has just appeared from one that has carried the whole match.
age.body: This is one figure standing for two different facts, and the row's own details say which of them you are looking at. For a TCP connection the operating system knows when it was established and reports it, so the age is the connection's own — a real fact about the connection rather than about this app. UDP has no such thing: there is no connection to have been established, only datagrams going back and forth, so what can honestly be said is how long this application has been watched talking to that address. The two are never merged into one claim, because they answer differently — a match server watched for two minutes may have been carrying traffic for an hour before you started the monitor. What both are good for is the same thing: telling an endpoint that has just appeared from one that has been there all along, which is usually the difference between something changing and something that was always this way.

chart.title: The chart
chart.short: One line per endpoint over the time you have been watching. A break in a line is probes that did not come back.
chart.body: Time runs from the moment you started watching this application, and the drawing grows to the right until it fills the width. There is one line per endpoint, and each point is the *slowest* round trip inside its slot rather than the average — a spike is what you are looking for, so it is never smoothed away, which is also why a line usually sits above the mean in the row beside it. The slots are deliberately wider than the interval an endpoint is probed at: a finer slot would be empty whenever no probe happened to land in it, and an empty slot is drawn as a break, so a healthy endpoint would appear to be dropping packets. A break therefore means probes that did not come back. The vertical scale is logarithmic, because an application's endpoints span two orders of magnitude — a router inside your provider at a few milliseconds beside a server across an ocean — and on a linear scale one spike flattens every other line against the floor. Nothing is clipped. A dashed line is the route to an endpoint that answers nothing: the round trip to a router on the way there, not to the endpoint itself.

watching.title: What watching an application means
watching.short: Choosing one watches the whole application — its other processes, and anything it launches. Nothing inside them is ever read.
watching.body: An application is a set of processes, not the one you clicked: a launcher starts the game, an anti-cheat may restart it, and a desktop app like Discord runs half a dozen helpers. Choosing one therefore watches all of them, and adopts anything they start afterwards, which is what lets you arm the monitor before a match rather than scramble for the picker once it has begun. What is read is which addresses those processes talk to and how much data crosses each one — the operating system's own connection tables and flow events. Nothing is read from inside a process: not its memory, not its traffic's contents, not its protocol. That is a hard limit rather than a current state of the code, and it is why this app is invisible to anti-cheat systems.

warmup.title: Warming up
warmup.short: The first seconds of a capture are the least informative it will ever have, so figures that need a full window are left blank until they mean something.
warmup.body: Right after you pick an application, no window is full: jitter would be computed over a handful of samples, a loss percentage would have a denominator of three, the fallback chain is still trying probe kinds, and the passive figures need several updates before they say anything. Presenting all of that as measurement invites you to act on the worst numbers the session will ever produce, so the app withholds them and says how long is left. A round trip is not withheld — one reply is one real measurement, and the mean of a few is the mean of a few. **Nothing already certain waits.** Proven filtering, nothing getting through, an endpoint alive by its own traffic, a freeze: those are answers, and arriving fast is the point of them.

passive.title: The traffic itself
passive.short: Measured from data your game is already exchanging, without sending anything. Nothing here is a ping.
passive.body: These figures cost no packets: the operating system already counts what crosses each connection, so this is the only part of the page that describes the traffic you are actually playing over rather than a substitute for it. Nothing here is a ping, and the distinction matters — no request is timed against its answer. The operating system reports that data arrived, not what it was replying to. How evenly it arrives is what you feel as stutter, and it folds in whatever pace the server chose: a server that skipped a tick and a network that delayed one look identical from here. That is exactly why these sit beside the route rather than instead of it. Their disagreement is the diagnosis — a clean route with ragged arrivals points at the server, a ragged route with even arrivals usually means a router is deprioritising our probes rather than that anything is wrong.

pool.title: The game's own reference servers
pool.short: Other addresses belonging to the same game, probed rarely. All of them silent while your baselines are clean is what points at the game rather than at you.
pool.body: One unreachable game server is ambiguous: it could be the server, or the route to it, or you. Several addresses belonging to the same game, sitting in different places and all silent at once while everything else you can reach answers normally, is the only evidence on this page that points at the game's own infrastructure rather than at your path to it. The pool is built from two sources — addresses the game's operator publishes, which ship with the app and change only when it is updated, and addresses this machine has actually seen the game connect to, which are kept locally and expire after a few days because game server addresses rotate. A member that has never answered a probe is not counted: a game's match server answers nothing anyone can send, so its silence proves nothing either way. Most titles publish no reference addresses at all, and an application with none can neither report an outage nor rule one out — which you need to know before reading a verdict that stops at the route.

checks.title: The check strip
checks.short: One cell is one check of that service, oldest on the left. Colour is never the only signal — every cell carries its word.
checks.body: Each service on this page is checked on a slow, fixed cadence, and every check leaves one cell. Oldest sits on the left, newest on the right, so the strip reads left to right like a sentence. A cell is a fact rather than a verdict: it says what that single check produced — answered, answered slowly, no answer, refused, the probe was filtered, or your tunnel answered — and keeping those apart is the point, because a single colour on the card cannot. Pointing at a cell, or moving through the strip with the arrow keys, says when that check happened. What the strip is for is telling apart "one packet went missing twenty minutes ago" from "nothing has answered since", which is the difference between a service that is fine and one that is not.

medianRtt.title: Ping, median
medianRtt.short: The middle round trip across the members of a group, so one slow member does not speak for all of them.
medianRtt.body: Wherever several things are measured together — the members of a baseline, the front doors of one service — the headline is the median across the ones that answered, not the average. With an average a single member on a bad path drags the figure away from what the others are actually doing, and the finding here is almost always which of them is reachable rather than what the arithmetic mean is. The distribution beside it says how the members disagree, and each of them carries its own figures below, so nothing is hidden by the roll-up.

latestCheck.title: Ping, last check
latestCheck.short: The round trip of the single most recent check — not an average of the strip beside it.
latestCheck.body: One check, the newest one, and nothing else folded in. It is here because it answers "how is it responding right now", which an average over the last quarter of an hour cannot: a service that has just started answering slowly still has a fast mean. Reading it as an average is the mistake this label exists to prevent — the mean is the figure beside it, over a stated window, and the strip shows how the checks in between actually went.

meanRtt.title: Ping, mean
meanRtt.short: The average round trip over the whole window the strip covers. One slow check barely moves it.
meanRtt.body: The average of every check in the stated window, which is the same stretch of time the strip beside it draws. Where the last check tells you how the service is answering at this moment, this tells you how it has been answering — and the gap between the two is itself informative: a last check far above the mean is the beginning of something, while the two sitting together means whatever you are seeing has been going on for a while.

egress.title: Which adapter it leaves by
egress.short: The network adapter this application's traffic uses — Wi-Fi, Ethernet, a VPN or an accelerator.
egress.body: The app binds its probes to the same local address your application's own traffic leaves from, so they follow the same route through any VPN or accelerator. Naming the adapter is what lets you check a before-and-after comparison: turn the VPN on, and this should change. Where the probe cannot be made to follow — another monitored application reaches the same endpoint by a different route, or the address was already being measured for something else — the row says so plainly rather than quietly measuring the wrong path.

tunnel.title: Through a tunnel
tunnel.short: A VPN or proxy on this machine carries this traffic, so the round trip is measured end to end through it rather than by a ping.
tunnel.body: A tunnel client running on your machine answers a great deal by itself. Send it a ping meant for a game server on another continent and its own software replies, in well under a millisecond, without a packet ever leaving your computer. The same is true of a bare connection attempt. Those numbers look wonderful and mean nothing, so this app refuses them: an endpoint marked this way is measured with a full exchange instead, which the tunnel has to carry to the real server and back before it can answer. That figure is honest, and it is the round trip your traffic actually experiences — the tunnel included, because the tunnel is genuinely in the way. It is not comparable with a figure measured without one, which is exactly why the badge is here. The app finds the tunnel two ways: it asks the system which adapter your packets would leave by, and it checks whether replies arriving from far-away addresses have really travelled. A reply that crossed no router on the way back did not come from another continent. Nothing here sends traffic outside your tunnel to compare, because that would show your provider what your tunnel exists to hide.

network.title: Whose network it is
network.short: The company whose network answers at this address — a hosting provider, a game operator, or your own internet provider.
network.body:
Every address on the internet belongs to a network that somebody runs, and knowing who that is turns a row of numbers into something you can act on. "Amazon" or "Google Cloud" beside a game server means the match is running in a data centre. Your own provider’s name on a router in the route means the traffic has not left their network yet, so a problem that far is theirs. A transit company you have never heard of usually means the traffic has crossed a border.

The name comes from a directory of networks that ships inside the app. Nothing is looked up over the internet: asking a remote service to name each address would tell that service which servers you are playing on, and this app does not do that to you. The cost of carrying it instead is that it is a photograph of one day — the date it was taken is in Settings — so a block of addresses that has changed hands since may still be named for whoever held it before.

The registration country is not a location. It is the country the network was registered in, which for a large provider is often nowhere near the machine that answered: an address announced from dozens of cities at once has one registration and many locations. Judge distance by the measured round trip, never by this.

Where a name is missing, nothing is known about that address and nothing is guessed in its place. The whole directory can be switched off in Settings, which frees about 12 MB of memory.

verdict.label: What the measurements add up to
verdict.notEnoughEvidence: Not enough measured yet to say
verdict.nothingMeasurable: Probes are being filtered — nothing could be measured
verdict.clear: Nothing points at a network-wide problem
verdict.localNetworkOrProvider: Services inside your country are failing too — your connection or your provider
verdict.crossBorderPath: Services inside your country answer and services abroad do not — the path out
verdict.routeToThisApplication: The network is fine and this application's own endpoints are not — the route it takes
verdict.gameServersUnreachable: The game's own reference servers are not answering from here
verdict.gameServersPartlyUnreachable: Part of the game's reference servers are not answering from here

advice.localNetworkOrProvider: Check your own equipment first; if that is fine, the problem is upstream of you and a VPN will not help.
advice.crossBorderPath: A VPN may help, since the failure is on the way out rather than on your own line.
advice.routeToThisApplication: A game accelerator may help: everything else reaches the network normally and this application's traffic does not.
advice.gameServers: Nothing on your side would change this. The addresses that belong to this game are not answering from here.

settings.languageHint: More languages are added as data; no part of the app has to change.
settings.countryHint: Chooses the domestic baseline list. Nothing is detected from the network — this app never asks anyone where you are.
settings.intervalHint: How often each baseline target is probed. Longer intervals leave more of the probe budget for the applications you monitor.

settings.rememberGameServersHint: Kept on this machine and sent nowhere. It is what lets the app tell "this game's servers are down" apart from "you cannot reach them". Turning it off deletes what was already remembered.
settings.privacyNote: All measurements stay on this machine. The app sends nothing anywhere except the probes on these lists.
